title: {{NAME}} and the Thunderfoot Cup
moral: Respecting a worthy opponent makes victory mean something, and makes defeat worth learning from.

pages.content:
The Thunderfoot Cup was played on a plateau of red volcanic rock in a valley that appeared on no modern map, which was the traditional qualification for venues of this particular significance. {{NAME}} had been selected by the valley itself: a tremor had found him in the carpark of a regular football match and led him, step by curious step, along a trail that ended here, where the pitch was enormous, the goals were standing stones, and every other player was a dinosaur.

The pitch was divided into two halves by a line of smaller stones. One half was occupied by the resident team, the Redrock Raptors, three velociraptors of considerable technical skill who were currently completing a training routine of such precise coordination that {{NAME}} could only watch with his hands on his hips and his mouth pursed in a long, slow whistle.

The other team, which was apparently {{NAME}}'s team, consisted of a stegosaurus named Bram who played in goal because she could not physically miss the opening, a jovial ankylosaur named Dolly who played defence with particular enthusiasm, and an empty space where the striker was supposed to be.

The space where the striker was supposed to be was, it appeared, {{NAME}}'s space.

pages.content:
The Raptors were called Kiv, Sela, and the captain, a longer-clawed velociraptor named Crest. Crest had the quality shared by all truly excellent players: she made difficult things look inevitable. She had been winning the Thunderfoot Cup for nine consecutive years.

Dolly introduced {{NAME}} to the team with enormous goodwill and a tail-wag that briefly knocked him sideways. Bram sized him up from the goal with the dispassionate assessment of someone who had seen a great many strikers come and go.

'Small,' Bram observed.

'Fast, though,' {{NAME}} said. This was true. He was the fastest player in his school league by a measurement that other players found demoralising.

Bram's expression did not change. But one eye-ridge lifted fractionally. 'Crest ran through a boulder once,' she said. 'Not around it. Through it.'

{{NAME}}'s face did not change either. His jaw set. His eyes went bright and focused in the way they did before a match that mattered. 'Then I'd better not stand still,' he said.

Dolly headbutted him gently in the side in what was clearly an expression of deep approval.

pages.content:
The match was the most extraordinary forty-five minutes of {{NAME}}'s life, and he had once spent an afternoon in a room full of hatching turtle eggs.

The Raptors were extraordinary. Kiv passed with frightening precision. Sela's footwork was faster than the eye could track. And Crest played with a complete, terrible certainty that the ball would go exactly where she intended, which it did, always.

But {{NAME}} was fast. Genuinely, startlingly fast. And he had a quality that even Crest, in forty-five minutes of trying, could not entirely account for: he made decisions before the situation required them. He was always half a second ahead, moving into space that had not yet opened, finding angles that had not yet appeared.

He scored twice: once with a left-foot curler that Crest's goalkeeper, a compact velociraptor, got a claw to but could not keep out, and once with a volley from the top of the volcanic rock penalty area that went in under the standing stone's lintel with a crack that echoed off every wall in the valley.

Crest stopped in the middle of the pitch and watched the second goal go in. Then she turned and looked at {{NAME}} with an expression he had never seen on a velociraptor before: pure, uncomplicated respect.

pages.content:
The score at half time was two-all. In the second half, Crest came back changed: not quieter, not less skilled, but more generous. She began to play with Kiv and Sela in ways she had not done in the first half, finding them in space, making them better. It was as if {{NAME}}'s second goal had reminded her what a great player was actually for.

The Raptors scored two more. So did {{NAME}}'s team, with Dolly of all creatures heading in a corner kick with a precision that surprised everyone including Dolly. The match ended four-four, and the Thunderfoot Cup, by ancient ruling, was therefore shared.

Crest walked to the centre of the pitch and stood there until {{NAME}} came to her. She was taller than him by a considerable margin. She looked down at him with those sharp, clear eyes and made a short, low sound that Dolly translated, with evident emotion, as 'well met, striker.'

{{NAME}} put out his hand. Crest looked at it, looked at him, and then bumped her clawed fist against his fist with deliberate care.

Bram let out a sound from the goal that echoed through the entire valley.

pages.content:
The valley held a shared meal after the match, which involved plants that {{NAME}} could not identify but which tasted of warm summer evenings and something he had no name for but would remember for the rest of his life.

Bram had left the goal and settled in the middle of the pitch in the comfortable way of large creatures with nowhere more pressing to be. Dolly had fallen deeply asleep against Bram's broad side, which looked extremely comfortable. Kiv and Sela were doing a slow, casual passing exercise in the fading light, and Crest sat alone at the pitch's edge looking at the valley with the particular expression of someone reviewing a day they are satisfied with.

{{NAME}} went and sat near her. Not next to her: near her. The distinction seemed right.

The standing-stone goals caught the last horizontal light and turned to gold. The volcanic rock cooled and clicked around them. {{NAME}}'s eyes grew heavy, his boots finally still after everything they had carried him through today.

Goodnight, number four. Dream of open pitches and fast feet, and wonder whether Crest would offer a rematch.
